issues.issue: Placing risk of loss on Seller until delivery of the deed conflicts with §6, where Buyer agrees to accept the Property in the condition existing on the closing date "including all faults ... whether now or hereafter existing." The two clauses allocate post-signing casualty to opposite parties.

"Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear" and "an appropriate deduction from the purchase price" set no measurable standard, and the clause does not say who chooses between repair and price reduction. Both the trigger and the election are open.

"Substantial" is defined circularly as any portion that "would impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Real Property" — a formula under which almost any taking qualifies — and "Real Property" is not the defined term "Property." The parenthetical also ends with a period, leaving the operative sentence a fragment.

"Insubstantial" is defined as a portion that "would not impair or otherwise affect the intended use," so on a literal reading of "affect" virtually no taking is insubstantial and this clause never operates. The line between this clause and the substantial-taking clause is unworkable as drawn.

The right of entry runs "during the period of this Option including any extension periods," but this instrument is a purchase agreement with a ninety-day closing under §8, the Option being a separate 2006 agreement referred to in §24. The duration of the inspection right cannot be fixed from this Agreement.

This sentence obliges "Optionee" to satisfy "Optionor," terms that appear nowhere else and are not defined; the preamble defines only "Seller" and "Buyer." Who owes the insurance obligation to whom must be inferred.

The notice obligation runs from "Optionee" to "Optionor," parties not defined anywhere in this Agreement, which names only Seller and Buyer in the preamble and in §14 Notices. The obligor of this notice duty is not identified by the instrument.

The "If to Buyer:" block is left entirely blank, so the Agreement supplies no notice address for one of the two parties. Every notice provision keyed to delivery "as provided above" is unworkable as to Buyer.

The deemed-receipt rule covers only mail and overnight courier, saying nothing about personal delivery, which the preceding notices clause expressly authorises as method (ii). When a hand-delivered notice takes effect is left unprovided for.

"No commission or other amount is payable to any other person or entity" uses "other" with no antecedent, since no broker is named. The reach of "or other amount" beyond brokerage is likewise unbounded.

Making time of the essence in "every provision hereof in which time is an element" is hard to apply where key dates are blank or indeterminate — the undated execution in the preamble driving §8's ninety-day closing, and §4's cure period. Strict time compliance is demanded of deadlines the instrument does not fix.

Section 22 requires amendments to be "in writing and executed by each party hereto," while §24 provides that the Agreement "may be amended only by written instrument, executed by the Buyer, Seller and the Government, acting by GSA." Whether GSA's signature is needed to amend is a direct conflict between the two clauses.

Survival is measured to "completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy" by GSA, but no provision of this Agreement obliges anyone to build improvements or to obtain such acceptance, and §6 has Buyer take the Property as-is. The endpoint of survival cannot be located within the instrument.

The clause says the Agreement "cancels and supersedes all prior agreements, whether written, oral, or both" and in the same breath preserves the August 2006 Real Estate Option Agreement as one of "the only agreements between parties hereto respecting the Property." Whether the Option survives as an operative agreement is contradicted within the provision itself; the Option's date is also left blank.

The disclaimer of representations "other than those expressly contained herein" sits uneasily with the preceding sentence of §24, which makes the Real Estate Option Agreement an operative agreement, and with §3, which takes the Permitted Exceptions from that Option. Whether "herein" includes the Option is left open.

Requiring every amendment to be executed by the Government acting by GSA conflicts with §22, which requires only that amendments be "executed by each party hereto" — GSA not being a party to this Agreement. The two amendment formalities cannot both control.

Section 26 states flatly that gas among other utilities is installed and available for immediate connection without special charge, whereas §7(c) makes the same representation without gas and only "for its current use." The two representations about the same utilities differ in scope and qualification.

The sentence makes utility terminations and relocations "the sole responsibility of Buyer" but limits Buyer's assumption of costs to those "after closing," leaving pre-closing relocation costs unallocated; the stray "8" is a page artifact in the text. The two limbs of the same sentence do not cover the same ground.

"Will cooperate ... to secure all necessary government approvals" states no standard of effort and no benchmark for compliance, and "any other applicable grant and/or loan programs" is an open-ended catch-all after the specific Brownfield Plan. The extent of Seller's duty cannot be measured.

This sentence duplicates the closing sentence of §2 but reduces the repayment by "any setoff" where §2 says "less any deductions," and no setoff is identified anywhere in the Agreement despite §2's promise of "setoffs as described below." Which reduction concept governs the Buyer's entitlement to the TIF reimbursement is unresolved.
